1058.title: the ranges ahead
1058.hook: three friends photograph the same peak from three valleys and argue over whether it's one mountain
1058.howItsDone: Hindu thought is taught through distinct schools, the darshanas, each with its own root texts and commentaries, and some students learn several of them side by side.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ranges ahead, and a hymn that ends or perhaps not. Your line was the ranges ahead. Did you let one question stay open instead of rushing it shut? Day one thousand fifty-eight.

Three friends go hiking on the same weekend, in three different valleys, and each one posts a photo of the big peak. In the first, it's a sharp tooth of rock. In the second, a long white shoulder. In the third, two summits side by side. The comments fill up. That can't be the same mountain. It is, though. Same rock, same snow, three valleys. Each photo is true, and none of them is the whole thing. Next year, the path spends weeks in a range like that. Today, another of the ranges ahead: the schools of thought, and a Rig Veda line about one truth seen from many valleys.
screen: `ONE PEAK, THREE VALLEYS.` → `EACH PHOTO TRUE.` → `NONE OF THEM THE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: The schools are called darshanas, and darshana is a word for seeing. It's the same word people use when they go to a temple for darshan, to see the deity and, some say, to be seen. So a darshana is a way of seeing, a view. Next year the path takes them one at a time. Nyaya, which asks how we know anything at all. Vaisheshika, which looks for the smallest parts of things. Samkhya, which sets awareness beside matter. Yoga, which you've met, the stilling of the mind. Mimamsa, which finds meaning in ritual. And Vedanta, which asks about Brahman and the Self. The promise of the outline is plain: each one is a lens for a week, and none of them is ranked. That doesn't mean the schools agreed. Their teachers argued, sometimes sharply, in long commentaries, and the path will let them argue. And there's a much older line, in the Rig Veda, that fits that valley-by-valley way of looking. In paraphrase: they call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni; the One that is, the sages call by many names. The Sanskrit is short enough to keep: ekam sat, the one that is, and bahudha vadanti, they speak of it in many ways. Readers hear that verse differently. Some hear it about the gods of the hymns, one reality behind many names. Some hear it more widely. Either way, it gives the coming year a shape: many valleys, many photos, and a mountain no single photo holds.
screen: `DARSHANA: A WAY OF SEEING.` · `ONE SCHOOL A WEEK, NONE RANKED.` · `THE SCHOOLS ARGUED.` · `THE ONE THAT IS, CALLED BY MANY NAMES.` · then, large: `MANY VALLEYS, ONE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one thing, seen more than one way. Choose something near you, a cup, a plant, your own hand. Look at it for a few breaths. Then close the eyes and know it another way: the sounds around it, its weight, the warmth or coolness you remember. Then think of where it came from, and who touched it before you. Same thing, three views, and none of them the whole. If you pray, you can let one of the names you use for God rest in the mind while you sit. If you don't, stay with the thing in front of you. The bell holds the time.
The ranges ahead. The years still to climb. Among them, the schools of thought, each a way of seeing, taken one valley at a time.
Your line: the ranges ahead. Today, when someone sees a thing differently from you, ask what their valley looks like before you say what yours does. Day one thousand fifty-eight.

1059.title: the ranges ahead
1059.hook: a young man comes home from his studies proud, and his father asks one question he can't answer
1059.howItsDone: The dialogue between Uddalaka and Shvetaketu in the Chandogya Upanishad is taught in Vedanta as the setting of the saying tat tvam asi, and some Hindu teachers retell it as a lesson in a student's humility.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ranges ahead, and the schools of thought: one mountain, many valleys. Your line was the ranges ahead. Did you ask someone what their valley looked like? Day one thousand fifty-nine.

A son walks back into his father's house after years away at study. He has learned the Vedas. He carries himself like someone who has finished. The Chandogya Upanishad doesn't flatter him: it says he came home proud, thinking himself learned. His father, Uddalaka, asks one question, and the son, Shvetaketu, who knows so much, has no idea what his father means. Year two walked through this scene. Today it comes back, one day before the year closes, for a different reason: it's the doorway to the last of the ranges ahead, the great sayings. And it's a story about a student who thought he'd reached the top.
screen: `HOME FROM STUDY, PROUD.` → `ONE QUESTION FROM HIS FATHER.` → `NO IDEA WHAT HE MEANS.`

segments.voice: Here's the question, in paraphrase: did you ask for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known? Shvetaketu says, sir, what kind of teaching is that? So his father gives him a picture. By knowing one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. The pot, the cup, the lamp: the difference is a name, a way of speaking. What's real is the clay. Then comes the line that makes the scene. Shvetaketu says, in effect: surely my teachers didn't know this, or why wouldn't they have told me? Teach me, sir. That turn is the whole story in small. He came home finished. One question later, he's a beginner again, asking to be taught. What follows in the Upanishad is a long teaching, and inside it is a short phrase his father says to him: tat tvam asi, that you are. Tradition counts it among the great sayings. The path plans to give those sayings a week each, near the end of the fifth year. So here's why this scene belongs at the end of year three. A year closes tomorrow. It's tempting to walk back in the door like Shvetaketu, carrying what you've learned like a finished thing: the Mahabharata, the saints, the teachers, the practices. They are real, and they count. But the ranges ahead are full of teachings that haven't been heard yet. In the Upanishad, the real teaching starts only once he says teach me, sir.
screen: `THE TEACHING THAT MAKES THE UNHEARD HEARD.` · `ONE LUMP OF CLAY.` · `TEACH ME, SIR.` · `TAT TVAM ASI, AHEAD ON THE PATH.` · then, large: `A BEGINNER AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: come home as a beginner. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one thing this path taught you this year, a story, a line, a practice. Hold it up like the lump of clay. Don't recite it. Ask what's underneath it that you haven't heard yet. Then set it down and simply breathe, with nothing finished. If you pray, you can bring the words teach me to God in your own way. If you don't, let the question stay with you through the sit. The bell holds the time.
The ranges ahead. The years still to climb. Among them, the great sayings, and a student who came home finished and left a beginner.
Your line: the ranges ahead. Today, in one conversation, ask a question about something you think you already know, and listen like Shvetaketu did. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

1060.title: Year 3: year close
1060.hook: the summit sit: look back over the year, from the snake sacrifice to the candle flame
1060.howItsDone: Yudhishthira's answers to the Yaksha at the lake in the Mahabharata's Vana Parva are retold in Hindu homes and talks, and his answer about what is most wonderful is sometimes recalled at times of loss or looking back.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of the ranges ahead: Shvetaketu, home and proud, who became a beginner again with teach me, sir. Did you ask a question about something you thought you knew? Day one thousand sixty.

Day six hundred ninety-seven. A king's great snake sacrifice, and a storyteller who begins to tell the story of the Bharatas. That's where this year started. Since then: a vow that cost Bhishma everything, a house built to burn, a game of dice, and Draupadi's question that the hall could not answer. Years in the forest. A lake, and a voice asking questions before anyone could drink. A chariot between two armies, and a song. Then a baby carried across a flooded river, a hill lifted over a village in the rain, a flute. Then the saints singing, the teachers talking, and a small flame on a table. Today, the summit sit: year three, looked at whole.
screen: `DAY 697: THE SNAKE SACRIFICE.` → `A WAR, A SONG, A CHILD, A FLUTE.` → `THE YEAR, LOOKED AT WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Look at the shape of it. The year began with the Mahabharata as a serial: the cousins, the exile, the war, Bhishma on his bed of arrows, the last journey with a dog that would not be left behind. Then the Bhagavata's Krishna as a child in Vraja: the butter thief, the mouth with the whole universe inside it, Govardhan held up over the village. Then the saints of bhakti: Andal, Tukaram, Kabir, Mirabai, singing in their own languages. Then the modern teachers: Ramakrishna, Vivekananda, Ramana asking who am I, Tagore's song offerings. Then the lineage tracks, and the practices: breath, japa, yoga nidra, the gaze on a flame. A war, a child, a choir, a classroom, a quiet room. Now go back to the lake. In the Vana Parva, a voice from the water warns each brother who tries to drink. They drink anyway, and fall. Only Yudhishthira stops to answer its questions. One of them is: what is the most wonderful thing? His answer, in paraphrase: every day, living beings go to the house of Death, and the ones who remain want to stay forever. What could be more wonderful than that? It's a strange thing to hold at the top of a year. Yudhishthira's wonder is at how easily the living forget what they see every day. Another year has gone. Faces in the stories have come and gone, and some listeners will have lost someone real since day six hundred ninety-seven. A year of sits is a small way of not forgetting: noticing, day by day, that you are among the ones who remain, for now, and that the time is worth using.
screen: `THE GREAT STORY: A WAR AND A SONG.` · `A CHILD IN VRAJA, THEN THE SAINTS.` · `THE TEACHERS, THEN THE PRACTICES.` · `WHAT IS THE MOST WONDERFUL THING?` · then, large: `AMONG THE ONES WHO REMAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the summit sit. Sit tall, and let the breath settle. Let three faces from this year come to mind, without choosing too hard: maybe someone from the great story, someone who sang, someone who taught. Don't rank them. Let each one stand there for a breath. Then let them go, and notice the simplest thing: the breath is still coming. You are still here, among the ones who remain. If you pray, you can give thanks for the year in the words you already use. If you don't, let the breath be the thanks. The bell holds the time.
Year three. The great story, the child in Vraja, the saints, the teachers, and the practices, held together at the summit before the next ranges.
Your line: Year three, year close. Tonight, tell one story from this year to someone, at the table or on the phone, the way a storyteller at a sacrifice once did. Day one thousand sixty.

1061.title: year 3 · the ranges
1061.hook: this part of the path is still being planned: a map with a dotted line, and a verse about steps that are never lost
1061.tomorrow: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1061.howItsDone: Bhagavad Gita 2.40 is quoted by some Hindu teachers to encourage people who are just starting a practice or who have fallen away from one, as a promise that no sincere effort on the path is wasted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Year 3, the year close: the great story, the child in Vraja, the saints, the teachers, and the lake where the living forget they are the ones who remain. Which story did you tell? Today is the last day of year three. Day one thousand sixty-one.

On a trail map, there's a moment where the solid red line turns into a dotted one. The trail goes on. Someone has walked it and marked it. But the map is saying, honestly, the details here are still being worked out. That's where the path stands tonight. The next ranges are drawn: the goddess, Shiva, the schools of thought, the Vedas, the women of the epics, the regional traditions. The lessons themselves are still being written and checked. So the last day of year three is a good day for one honest verse about walking into a dotted line.
screen: `THE SOLID LINE TURNS DOTTED.` → `THE RANGES ARE DRAWN.` → `THE LESSONS STILL BEING WRITTEN.`

segments.voice: The verse is from the Bhagavad Gita, in the second chapter, which this year re-read in its place on the battlefield. Krishna has just told Arjuna he's about to hear a new way of understanding action. And before he explains it, he gives a promise. In paraphrase: on this path, no effort begun is lost, and no harm comes of it. Even a little of this dharma protects you from great fear. Hold that next to a dotted line on a map. The Gita doesn't say finish the path and then you'll be safe. It says even a little of it protects. Some teachers read that generously: the half-managed sit, the missed week, the story whose ending slipped away, none of it is wasted. In the verse's own picture, whatever was walked stays walked. Commentators read the verse in more than one way. Some hear it about the steadied mind Krishna is about to describe: action done without grasping at results. Others hear it about any honest start on a spiritual path. Either way, it's a verse made for beginnings. And year three has been full of people who walked into country no one had mapped for them. Yudhishthira at a lake with a voice in the water. Mirabai walking out of palace rules. Ramana, a boy who left home for a holy hill. Tomorrow the path begins year four with the Devi, the goddess, and a text read from start to finish. A new range, and an old promise to carry into it: whatever was walked stays walked.
screen: `A DOTTED LINE ON THE MAP.` · `NO EFFORT ON THIS PATH IS LOST.` · `EVEN A LITTLE PROTECTS FROM GREAT FEAR.` · `YEAR FOUR BEGINS WITH THE DEVI.` · then, large: `WHAT WAS WALKED STAYS WALKED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand at the edge of the map. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one small thing you did on this path this year, even something you think didn't count: one sit, one story, one minute of attention. Let it be enough. Then turn, gently, to face what's ahead, without planning it. Just the next step, and the breath that carries you there. If you pray, you can bring the coming year before God, or the goddess, in your own words. If you don't, let tomorrow have a little room. The bell holds the time.
Year three. The great story and the saints, now walked, and kept. And the ranges beyond it, drawn on the map, still being written.
Your line: year three, the ranges. Today, take one small step on something you'd set aside, and let it count, even if it's only a little. Day one thousand sixty-one. Year three, done.

1062.title: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1062.hook: a king who has lost everything and a merchant thrown out by his own family meet in a forest, and neither can stop worrying
1062.carry: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1062.tomorrow: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1062.howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the Devi Mahatmya, also called the Chandi or Durga Saptashati, from beginning to end, especially during Navaratri, and it is recited in some temples devoted to the goddess.

segments.voice: Yesterday was the last day of year 3: the ranges, and the Gita's promise that no effort on this path is lost. What small step did you take? Today year four begins, with the goddess. Day one thousand sixty-two.

A king rides into a forest alone. He has lost his kingdom. Enemies beat him in battle, and then his own ministers turned on him and took the treasury. He tells himself he's out hunting. In the forest he finds a quiet hermitage, the home of a sage named Medhas, and he stays. And there, under the trees, he can't stop worrying. Is my elephant being fed? Are my servants treated well? Is the treasure I gathered being wasted? Then he meets a second man, a merchant named Samadhi, sitting there just as lost. That's how the Devi Mahatmya begins. Year four reads it whole, from its first page to its last.
screen: `A KING RIDES INTO A FOREST ALONE.` → `HE CAN'T STOP WORRYING.` → `A MERCHANT, JUST AS LOST.`

segments.voice: Devi Mahatmya means the glory of the goddess. Tradition places it inside a larger book, the Markandeya Purana, and it's also known as the Chandi. In some homes and temples it's recited from beginning to end. But notice what it opens with. Not a goddess. Two men with a problem they can't solve. The merchant's story is harder than the king's. His own wife and sons, greedy for his money, threw him out of the house. And still, he tells the king, he can't stop wondering whether they're well. Are they happy? Are they in trouble? Why does his mind keep going back to people who sent him away? So the two of them go to the sage together with one honest question. In paraphrase: we both know these things have left us. We know it. So why do we still grieve? Why doesn't knowing help? Medhas doesn't call them foolish. He points at birds: hungry themselves, they still drop grain into the beaks of their young. Every creature, he says, is pulled this way. Then he gives the pull a name. Mahamaya, the great illusion, and in this text she is the goddess herself. She seizes the minds of even the wise and drags them into confusion. And the same goddess, when she is gracious, is the one who sets people free. That's the surprise of the opening. The goddess isn't introduced first as a warrior. She's introduced as the power at work inside the very worry the king and the merchant carried into the forest. The king asks the obvious next question: who is this goddess? And Medhas begins to tell stories. The rest of the book is those stories.
screen: `TWO MEN WITH A PROBLEM.` · `WHY DOESN'T KNOWING HELP?` · `BIRDS FEEDING THEIR YOUNG.` · `MAHAMAYA BINDS, AND SETS FREE.` · then, large: `WHO IS THIS GODDESS?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one thing your mind keeps going back to. Settle, and let the breath slow. Let it come up on its own: a person, a place, a job, something that's gone and still pulls. Don't argue with it, and don't try to fix it. Just notice the pull, the way the merchant noticed his. Where do you feel it in the body? Each time you breathe out, let the grip loosen a little, without throwing away the care underneath it. If you pray, you can hold it before God or the goddess in the words you already use. If you don't, let the breath do the holding. The bell holds the time.
The Devi Mahatmya. The glory of the goddess: a book that begins in a forest, with two men who can't stop worrying, and a sage who names the pull.
Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Today, when your mind goes back to something that's gone, notice the pull once, kindly, and keep walking. Day one thousand sixty-two. Year four, begun.

screen: `DAY 1062 COUNTS.` → `YEAR 4, BEGUN.` → `TOMORROW: THE DEVI MAHATMYA (13 CHAPTERS, READ WHOLE).`

1063.title: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1063.hook: the first story: Vishnu asleep on the waters, two demons rising, and Brahma praising the goddess who is Vishnu's sleep
1063.carry: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1063.tomorrow: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
1063.howItsDone: Brahma's praise of Yoganidra in the first chapter of the Devi Mahatmya is recited as part of the whole text, and some Hindus who recite the Chandi treat the first chapter as its own opening section.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Devi Mahatmya opened in a forest: a king and a merchant who couldn't stop worrying, and a sage who named the pull Mahamaya. Did you notice a pull of your own? Day one thousand sixty-three.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `TWO MEN IN A FOREST.`

segments.voice: No land. No sky to speak of. Only water, everywhere, at the end of an age. On that water, Vishnu lies asleep on the great serpent. From his navel grows a lotus, and on the lotus sits Brahma, the creator. And then, out of the dirt in Vishnu's ears, two demons are born: Madhu and Kaitabha. They look around, see Brahma on his flower, and decide to kill him. Brahma looks down at Vishnu, the one who could protect him. Vishnu doesn't move. He's fast asleep. This is the first story the sage Medhas tells the king and the merchant, and the goddess is in it from the start, though not where you'd look.
screen: `ONLY WATER, AT THE END OF AN AGE.` → `TWO DEMONS RISE.` → `VISHNU WON'T WAKE.`

segments.voice: Brahma doesn't shake Vishnu. He doesn't call Vishnu's name. He turns to the sleep itself. In this text Vishnu's sleep has a name, Yoganidra, and she is the goddess. So Brahma praises her. In paraphrase, he says: you hold up this world, you create it, you protect it, and at the end you take it back. You are the great knowledge and the great illusion. You are the dark night at the end of things, and you are beauty and modesty and understanding. Who could praise you enough, when you even put Vishnu himself to sleep? And then a request: wake him, and confuse these two demons. The goddess answers. The text describes her drawing out of Vishnu's eyes, his mouth, his nostrils, his arms, his heart, his chest. And Vishnu wakes. He fights the two demons for a very long time. Then the strangest moment. Confused by the great illusion, the demons, proud of their strength, tell Vishnu they're pleased with him, and he may ask them for a boon. Vishnu asks: be killable by me. They're caught. So they look around, see water in every direction, and add a condition, in paraphrase: then kill us where the earth is not covered with water. Vishnu lifts them onto his thigh, dry ground above the flood, and kills them there. Look at what the story is teaching about the goddess. She isn't a helper standing next to Vishnu. She's the power inside his sleeping and his waking. Even the god of preserving the world rests in her. And the same confusion the merchant felt yesterday is at work in the demons today: two strong beings, outwitted by their own pride.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch sleep let go. Sit or lie comfortably. Close the eyes. Then follow the order the text gives as the goddess leaves Vishnu: let attention return to the eyes behind the lids, then the mouth, the nose and its breath, the arms, the heart, the chest. One place at a time, notice it waking. No need to force alertness. Just let each part be here. If you pray, you can greet the morning, or this moment, in words you already use. If you don't, let the breath be the greeting. The bell holds the time.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, its first story: the goddess as Yoganidra, the sleep of Vishnu, who leaves him so he can wake.
Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Tomorrow morning, before you reach for anything, take one breath and notice yourself waking, one part at a time. Day one thousand sixty-three.

1064.howItsDone: Images of Durga in temples and in festival pandals during Navaratri and Durga Puja can show her many arms holding the weapons the gods gave her, riding a lion, as told in the Devi Mahatmya's second chapter.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, Vishnu slept on the waters until Brahma praised the goddess who was his sleep, and two demons died on dry ground they never saw coming. Did you notice yourself waking this morning? Day one thousand sixty-four.

A trident. A discus. A conch shell. A spear. A bow and two quivers of arrows. A thunderbolt, and a bell taken from an elephant's neck. A staff. A noose. A string of prayer beads and a water pot. A sword and a shield. An axe. Jewels, and a garland that never fades. A drinking cup. A snake to wear around the neck. And a lion. That's the inventory of the second story in the Devi Mahatmya. From the summit, at the end of year three, this path glimpsed the moment it begins: the gods defeated by the buffalo demon Mahisha, their anger pouring out as light, and the light becoming a goddess. Today we read on. What does everyone give her?
screen: `A TRIDENT, A DISCUS, A CONCH.` → `A CUP, A SNAKE, A LION.` → `WHAT DOES EVERYONE GIVE HER?`

segments.voice: In the second chapter, once the goddess has taken form, the gods line up to give. And each gift comes out of the giver's own thing. Shiva draws a trident from his trident. Vishnu brings a discus out of his discus. Varuna, the lord of the waters, gives a conch and a noose. Agni, fire, gives a spear. Indra gives a thunderbolt from his own thunderbolt, and a bell from his elephant. Brahma gives prayer beads and a water pot. The sun fills the pores of her skin with his rays. The ocean of milk gives jewels and clothes that never wear out. Kubera, lord of wealth, gives a full drinking cup. And Himavat, the Himalaya, the mountain itself, gives her a lion to ride. Notice how the first gifts are given. Shiva, Vishnu and Indra don't hand over a spare. Each draws a copy out of his own weapon, from his own power. She doesn't take their strength away. She carries all of it at once. Then she laughs, a long loud laugh, and the sky fills with the sound. The earth shakes. Mountains rock. The demons look up and rush toward the noise, and they see her, filling the three worlds with her light. The battle starts. Mahisha's generals come at her with armies. And here the chapter gives one more detail worth keeping: as she fights, the breaths she lets out become troops, whole armies of helpers, beating drums and blowing conches. She breathes, and allies appear. Her lion shakes its mane and stalks through the enemy. And the chapter ends with the generals' armies in ruins, and Mahisha still to come.
screen: `EACH GIFT FROM THE GIVER'S OWN.` · `THE MOUNTAIN GIVES A LION.` · `SHE LAUGHS, AND THE EARTH SHAKES.` · `HER BREATHS BECOME ARMIES.` · then, large: `SHE CARRIES ALL OF IT AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count the gifts you carry. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind two or three people who gave you something of their own: a way of cooking, a habit of patience, a laugh, a skill with their hands. Let each one stand there for a few breaths, and name what they gave. Then notice that you carry all of it at once, right now, sitting here. And with each long breath out, let something of that come forward. If you pray, you can give thanks for them in the words you already use. If you don't, let the breath carry the thanks. The bell holds the time.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, its second story: a goddess armed with each god's own gift, riding the mountain's lion, whose very breaths become armies.
Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Today, give someone a copy of something that's really yours: a recipe, a trick, a song, a way of doing things. Day one thousand sixty-four.
